title: High School Contemporaries Allard Lowenstein and Roy Cohn as Two Distinct Sides of America’s Character
author: Daniel Warner
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-20-at-1.09.51-PM-680x473.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/21/high-
school-contemporaries-allard-lowenstein-and-roy-cohn-as-two-distinct-sides-of-
americas-character/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-20-at-1.09.51-PM-680x473.png)

Allard Lowenstein at congressional race fundraiser, August 29, 1976 - Public
Domain

Few people would associate Allard Lowenstein with Roy Cohn. Lowenstein tried
to influence politics while avoiding the problems of dirty hands. Cohn was the
ultimate insider, one who gloried in all the underhanded tricks that soil
politics, “the master of situational immorality,” and the man who taught
Donald Trump how braggadocio and underhandedness were the secrets to success.
And yet they both had something in common: they both attended the Horace Mann
School in New York City, my alma mater.

I have often thought of them as two sides of the American coin. Lowenstein
represented one tradition: public service and a belief that politics could be
used in the service of a larger common good. Cohn represented self-interest,
power, and the conviction that politics was ultimately a struggle in which
winning mattered more than the rules by which one played.

Roy Cohn graduated from Horace Mann in 1944, Lowenstein in 1945. The Class of
1944 had only 78 students, about the same number as the Class of 1945. For at
least a brief period, they were walking the same corridors, taught by many of
the same teachers, and shaped by the same intellectual world.

That coincidence has always fascinated me. How could the two have emerged from
the same milieu to represent such different visions of America?

Lowenstein and Cohn weren't just two distinct personalities; they were
products of different currents in postwar America. Lowenstein belonged to the
world of civil rights, liberal internationalism, antiwar politics, and reform.
Cohn belonged to the world of anti-Communism, McCarthyism, New York City power
politics, the man-about-town of the gossip columns, and eventually the
politics of personal influence.

Lowenstein and Cohn can be seen as opposing poles of the American character:
the aspiration toward something larger than oneself versus the relentless
pursuit of the self; the belief in politics as a means of serving others as
opposed to the belief in politics as a means of acquiring and exercising
power.

Lowenstein’s life was firmly grounded in the liberal politics of his time. “In
a sense, the theme of his [Al’s] life was, Let Right be Done,” wrote Douglas
Hunt after his death. President of the National Student Association, aide to
Hubert Humphrey and Robert Kennedy, participant in the Mississippi Freedom
Summer, leader of the “Dump Johnson” movement, briefly a member of Congress,
and later a leader of the anti-Vietnam War “Dump Nixon” movement, Lowenstein
repeatedly put his political talents at the service of causes larger than
himself. Jimmy Carter appointed him to the United Nations Commission on Human
Rights.

Cohn was the other side of the coin, the underside of the postwar euphoria. He
has recently become a figure of renewed interest as journalists continue to
investigate Trump’s rise and his early mentors. (See “How Roy Cohn taught
Donald Trump everything” by Kai Bird and Susan Goldmark in the August 3, 2026,
_New Yorker_ as well as their book about Cohn, _American Scoundrel_.)

There are three parts to Cohn’s career: Cohn the anti-Communist prosecutor;
Cohn the power broker and fixer; and Cohn as a precursor to the world of
Trump’s politics. In the first phase of his career, he was involved in the
prosecution of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg in 1951 as part of the anti-
Communist Red Scare after World War II. He was chief prosecutor in the Army-
McCarthy hearings, working closely with F.B.I. Director J. Edgar Hoover in
investigating supposed Communist influence in the U.S. Army. (Joseph Welch’s
famous “Have you no shame, sir,” to Senator McCarthy might well have been
directed at Roy Cohn.)

During much of his later career, Cohn was known as a fixer for people like
Donald Trump. “Cohn taught him [Trump] that the pyrotechnics of publicity were
more important than the law. What counted was controlling the narrative,” Bird
and Goldmark wrote in _The New Yorker_. Cohn was disbarred by a New York
appellate court in 1986 for professional misconduct involving dishonesty,
fraud, deceit, and misrepresentation.

What survives as Cohn’s legacy is his mentoring of people like Trump. Sam
Roberts, quoted in _The New Yorker_ article, called Cohn “a master of
situational immorality.” “He had rules about how to exercise power. . . . You
would always try to goad your enemies into being the worst they possibly could
be and then turn that against them, so that Roy Cohn would actually look like
the good guy, which he virtually never was.”

Despite the differences, there were similarities between the two men. Both
were ambitious. Both were highly intelligent. Both understood institutions.
Both were convinced that individuals could alter history. Both were willing to
fight. Both had strong egos. Each was, in his own way, intensely political;
each believed in the power of individuals to shape events.

The difference between them may have been what they believed those qualities
could be used for. Lowenstein was no naïve idealist. He understood politics,
worked within institutions, organized campaigns, challenged powerful men, and
served in Congress. But for him power was a means: a way of advancing causes
and ideals beyond himself. Cohn understood political reality equally well,
perhaps better. But his concept of power was very different. For Cohn, power
was not restrained by an overriding conception of the common good. It was
something to acquire, exercise, and use to win.

In that sense, the contrast between them was not simply idealism versus
realism. Both were political realists in the sense that they understood how
power worked. The deeper difference was what that power was for.

Are there really two poles in America’s character? Neither Lowenstein nor Cohn
was as absolute as I have portrayed them, although I do believe Cohn was much
more than just a “scoundrel.” What is noteworthy is how Lowenstein’s
idealistic liberalism has faded from the current radar screen while Cohn’s
version of realism has burst front and center.

What happens to a political culture when power increasingly becomes an end in
itself rather than a means to some conception of the common good? The motto of
the Horace Mann School is “Magna est veritas et prævalet,” “Great is the
truth, and it prevails.” The same school whose motto invokes truth produced
two men whose approaches to truth, power, and political life could hardly have
been more different.
